strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear statistical evidence that scientific abstracts have substantially denser nuggets (39.5% vs ~4% in other domains) and more complex event structures than existing datasets
Comprehensive dataset construction: Rigorous multi-stage annotation process with quality control across 2,508 documents and 24,381 events, with detailed schema design grounded in document structure

Strong experimental results: EXCEEDS consistently outperforms baselines on all metrics, with particularly strong hierarchical event extraction (EC F1: 47.60), and thorough analysis of performance across complex nugget types
Principled technical approach: Word-word event grid elegantly unifies encoding of nugget boundaries, event-argument links, and hierarchical relationships in an end-to-end framework

Comprehensive analysis: Detailed statistics on event/argument distributions, complex information forms, and comparison with established benchmarks provides strong motivation for domain-specific methods
weaknesses: Limited dataset scope: Only ACL papers (2019-2022) in NLP domain, not truly 'scientific domain'; only abstracts, not full papers; moderate size (2,508 docs) by modern standards; unclear generalization to other scientific fields (biology, chemistry, physics, medicine)

Missing critical quality metrics: No inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa) reported; only describes quality inspection procedures without quantitative validation; fundamental requirement for reproducible dataset contributions

Moderate method novelty: Grid-based token-pair relations adapted from prior work [12]; BiAttention and Biaffine are standard techniques; main contribution is combining existing techniques rather than introducing novel concepts

Problematic baseline comparisons: OneIE uses additional entity annotations others lack (unfair); BartGen and PAIE require external ED module; no comparison with recent LLM-based approaches despite claiming they are state-of-the-art; no statistical significance testing despite multiple runs

Inadequate ablation studies: Only ablates Biaffine and BiAttention modules; missing ablations on CLN, BiLSTM, grid design choices, and 3 heuristic inference rules; rules appear ad-hoc without justification (e.g., 'broken HTL chain' undefined)

Unresolved core challenges: Despite design goals, performance on complex nuggets remains poor (inconsecutive F1=25.34, reverse-ordered F1=18.54); these are 4% of nuggets but undermine claims of handling complexity; authors acknowledge difficulty but propose no solutions

Technical presentation issues: Batch size of 1 used without justification; hyperparameter choices (hidden size 1024, learning rates) not explained or ablated; no analysis of computational efficiency; unclear handling of abstracts exceeding BERT token limit

Incomplete reproducibility: Dataset/code promised on GitHub but status unclear; standard deviations/confidence intervals not reported; limited detail on hyperparameter selection; relatively small test set (250 documents)

Missing error analysis: No breakdown of which event types are most problematic; no qualitative case studies of failures; no cross-domain evaluation (news→scientific transfer); no inter-rater reliability on schema validity or environment classification

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of density and complexity challenges specific to scientific event extraction

High-quality dataset contribution (2,508 documents, 24,381 events) with rigorous quality control (73.05% first-pass acceptance), iterative schema refinement with domain experts, and comprehensive annotation protocol documentation

Intuitive and sound technical approach: word-word grid formulation elegantly unifies event detection and argument extraction while naturally handling hierarchical relations, discontinuous arguments, and long-distance dependencies

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 10+ baselines across architectural families, ablation studies, complex scenario analysis, and error analysis revealing that missed predictions dominate over boundary errors
State-of-the-art results with notable improvements on complex structure metrics (AC: +0.51%, EC: +0.53% over second-best baseline)
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear writing, extensive appendices with annotation protocol, hyperparameters, full results, and statistical analysis

Comparative analysis demonstrating SciEvents exhibits significantly higher information density (5.54 events, 12.82 arguments per 100 tokens) and more complex structures (33.70% overlapping, 25.63% sub-events) than existing datasets
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset scope: sourced exclusively from ACL conference abstracts (2019-2022) representing only NLP sub-domain; 'scientific domain' claims not validated across chemistry, biology, physics, or other scientific fields; generalizability fundamentally constrained

Core challenge incompletely addressed: despite dense/complex structures being primary motivation, performance on these remains poor (discontinuous: 13.86% F1, overlapping: 22.46% F1, reverse-order: 48.32% F1), suggesting grid formulation has fundamental limitations for stated problems

Critical omission: inter-annotator agreement (IAA) scores not reported; only first-pass inspection rate (73.05%) provided; cannot verify dataset consistency meets standards expected for training/evaluation benchmark

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: O(l²) complexity not contextualized; average document length ~175 tokens means 175×175 grid; behavior for longer documents (l=350+) unclear; training cost (0.0609 GPU hours/epoch) lacks baseline comparison

Methodological design choices lack justification: no explanation for 2D convolutions in grid refinement, no comparison with alternative structured representations (graphs, AMR), heuristic decoding with ontology constraints appears brittle, no sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters (e.g., K=2 refinement layers)

No cross-domain or transfer learning experiments: models trained on SciEvents not evaluated on biomedical/legal/clinical domains despite existing EE datasets; cannot determine if insights specific to ACL abstracts or generalizable to scientific domain; transfers to other domains untested

Limited theoretical justification for grid approach: beyond intuitive appeal, no formal analysis of why grid-based modeling should outperform alternatives; missing ablation comparing simpler pairwise classification; no visualization or interpretation of learned grid patterns

LLM evaluation insufficient: only one LLM baseline (KnowCoder with LLaMA 2-7B); no GPT-3.5/4 prompting experiments; LLMs not given equal tuning effort as EXCEEDS; doesn't reflect practical use cases of commercial LLM APIs

Evaluation metric limitations: exact span matching is strict without partial credit; no macro/micro F1 breakdown by event type; zero-threshold multi-label decision (Eq. 6) simplistic with no threshold sensitivity analysis

Reproducibility gaps: code availability status unclear; annotation tool shown only as Chinese screenshots; data release timeline unspecified; conservative training strategy (skip early validation) could mask convergence issues

Event correlation task feels disconnected: sub-events comprise only 25.63% of dataset; EC improvement smallest among metrics (0.53%); unclear if hierarchical structure is central or peripheral contribution

Limited analysis of why method works: insufficient intuition beyond grid formulation; no explanation for metric-specific improvements; missing qualitative examples showing grid advantages over baselines; no error type comparison with other methods
